title: Japan Poised to Ramp Up LNG Buying as Power Prices Surge | OilPrice.com

Japanese utilities may raise spot LNG cargo buying as surging electricity prices in recent days have made gas-fired power generation profitable for the first time since the Iran war began.

Japan’s physical spark spread, the difference between the price received by a power-generating facility for electricity produced, has turned positive on a seven-day average for the first time since the Middle East conflict began, data compiled by Bloomberg showed on Tuesday.

A positive spark spread means utilities will earn more from selling electricity compared to the price at which they would buy LNG.

Sure, LNG prices are at their four-year highs in both Asia and Europe amid the still severely disrupted LNG flows from Qatar via the Strait of Hormuz.

But power prices in Japan have also jumped, to the highest in more than four years.

Spot electricity prices in Japan surged on Monday to their highest level since August 2022 as gas demand is set to rise amid expectations of snowfall and colder weather in the coming days.

Snowfall and plunging temperatures this week will boost gas demand, while cloudy skies are set to reduce the potential of solar power generation in Japan, leaving the power system more reliant on natural gas, whose prices have soared this year due to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

Asia has sought to reduce gas demand where possible and is turning to coal for power generation where available, as the benchmark price for spot LNG delivery into North Asia has tripled from this time last year to about $30 per million British thermal units (MMBtu).

Japan’s high power prices, however, would now make importing and running more gas for electricity generation profitable for utilities. This could boost Japan’s appetite for LNG supply despite the high spot prices.

Japan is expected to overtake China as the world’s largest LNG importer this year, for the first time since 2022, as high LNG prices and comfortable storage levels in China limit purchases, analysts say.
